content: Congestive heart failure (CHF) is a complex clinical syndrome characterized by the heart's inability to pump sufficient blood to meet the metabolic demands of the body. This condition arises from dysfunction in various anatomical components of the heart, including the pericardium, myocardium, endocardium, heart valves, and great vessels. The symptoms of CHF are primarily due to inadequate forward blood flow to the body and backward flow into the lungs, leading to dyspnea, fatigue, and fluid retention. Physical examination often reveals signs such as pulmonary rales, peripheral edema, and jugular venous distension. Heart failure is classified based on ejection fraction into two main categories: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). HFpEF is associated with left ventricular (LV) remodeling, diastolic dysfunction, LV hypertrophy, impaired relaxation, endothelial dysfunction, and increased arterial and ventricular stiffness. Emerging models of HFpEF pathophysiology highlight the role of systemic microvascular endothelial inflammation, often driven by comorbidities such as diabetes, hypertension, obesity, smoking, and ischemia. In contrast, HFrEF pathogenesis is largely related to cellular proliferation and metabolic abnormalities. Common pathological processes in both HFpEF and HFrEF include altered excitation-contraction coupling, epigenetic modifications, sarcomeric protein changes, increased adrenergic drive, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation, nitric oxide insensitivity, ATP depletion, reactive oxygen species production, and elevated cell death rates. The causes of CHF can be broadly categorized into cardiac and non-cardiac origins. Cardiac causes include conditions such as aortic regurgitation, aortic stenosis, arrhythmias, atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, cardiomyopathies, valvular heart diseases, and congenital heart defects. Non-cardiac causes include anemia, thyroid dysfunction, and chronic lung diseases. CHF must be differentiated from other conditions that cause dyspnea, fatigue, and edema. Epidemiologically, CHF affects approximately 5 million people in the United States, with nearly 500,000 new cases diagnosed annually. It accounts for a significant portion of healthcare expenditures, with over 50% of patients requiring readmission within six months of treatment. The average hospital stay for CHF patients is six days. CHF is associated with a poor prognosis, with an annual mortality rate of approximately 10%. In the Framingham study, 80% of men and 70% of women under 65 years of age with CHF died within eight years of diagnosis. The diagnosis of CHF involves clinical assessment, history-taking, physical examination, and diagnostic tests. Classic symptoms include dyspnea, fatigue, and fluid retention. Patients may present with exercise intolerance, pulmonary congestion, or peripheral edema. The ejection fraction is typically below 35% in symptomatic systolic heart failure. Laboratory tests, including serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels, renal function tests, and thyroid function tests, are useful in diagnosing and monitoring CHF. Imaging studies such as chest X-rays, echocardiography, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) provide valuable information about cardiac structure and function. Echocardiography is particularly useful for assessing stroke volume, end-diastolic volume, and ejection fraction. Exercise stress testing and myocardial viability studies may also be employed to evaluate functional capacity and assess the potential for revascularization. Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) is a severe manifestation of CHF, characterized by acute shortness of breath due to pulmonary edema, hypotension, and impaired organ perfusion. ADHF requires aggressive treatment to improve oxygenation and hemodynamic stability. Initial management includes oxygen therapy, diuretics to reduce preload and intravascular volume, and vasodilators to decrease afterload. Chronic CHF therapy, such as ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and digoxin, is typically not initiated during acute episodes. General measures in CHF management include addressing the underlying cause, treating comorbid conditions, adhering to a low-salt diet, monitoring weight, and ensuring vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus. Diuretics are often the first step in managing volume overload, with loop diuretics, thiazides, and potassium-sparing diuretics being commonly used. Regular monitoring of renal function and electrolytes is essential to avoid complications such as hypokalemia or hyperkalemia. ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are the second step in CHF management, as they improve symptoms and reduce mortality by counteracting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. These medications are typically introduced after diuresis has been achieved or concurrently in stable patients.
